body: Spending some more time thinking about this I realize that the engine doesn't actually differentiate between "pixel" and "vertex" _lights_ and rather it's a material setting which means all lights are culled by the same rules and this is going to be a difficult issue to fix. A possible solution would be to have more lenient light culling or including an engine option to turn light culling off entirely (as far as I could find out no such settings exist) for projects that only use vertex lighting and don't mind the performance cost.

Looking at it a _third_ time with wireframe view shows that it _could_ be related to the order in which vertices are processed but this behavior (vertex goes off screen and so does the light) only appears at certain angles and not all

I just tested to and it seems your right. [#110184](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/110184) improves things a lot. But there are still certain angles where the light flickers a bit. 

The remaining flickering appears to be from cases where only one vertex of a triangle is in the cluster. Once that vertex is clipped, the whole triangle goes dark.

I concur that this improves the result, but there are still bugs and the behavior of vertex lighting in all renderers **and** the Forward+ renderer is still different/unique from the Mobile and Compatibility renderers.

I am certain that the overarching problem with **all** the renderers is that they do not take into account whether there are still lit vertices on screen when culling the lights. This is a unique problem to vertex lighting because with vertex lighting and large triangles you can have light "spilling over" far outside of the given range of a light and my guess is that whatever calculation or assumptions are being used to cull lights is based on pixel lighting where light does not spill outside of this range.

To give further evidence to this theory, using an OmniLight3D and setting its range to 4096 with higher attenuation and more energy to make it look like a shorter range light makes it so the light does not get culled the same way the lights in these clips do when using Mobile and Compatibility renderers. In fact, I think a bandaid solution to this problem would be to give the user the ability to mark a light as "Do Not Cull". This would obviously impact performance but would ensure that even triangles larger than the current screen (or triangles that extend behind/past the screen) would still get lit properly by off-screen lights regardless of camera angle.

That said, ideally a more proper and thorough solution to the issue would involve _not culling any lights while there are still vertices lit by them._ Whether this is actually possible I have no idea, but that is the root issue with vertex lighting right now in both Forward+, Mobile and Compatibility renderers. If desired I can create a new MRP that more clearly demonstrates this issue with some larger more bespoke geometry.

This has kept bothering me as the current state of vertex lighting makes it quite unusable, so I decided to download the Godot source and start digging around myself. Long story short culling is an overarching issue in every renderer and I'm still not exactly sure where the culling happens or by what metric but adding this line of code to [scene/3d/light_3d.cpp](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/scene/3d/light_3d.cpp#L467) immediately has the effect of "fixing" the issue in both Mobile and Compatibility renderers:
`RS::get_singleton()->instance_set_ignore_culling(get_instance(), true);`

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3cfb4081-ac9f-4b88-91b5-94760705df32

In other words, the lights are indeed getting culled while vertices are still being lit by them and I still propose that a real fix for this would involve letting the user add a cull margin (or indeed, turn culling off) for their respective geometry needs. Unfortunately, this only fixes the issue on Mobile and Compatibility.

On the Forward+ renderer even when the lights ignore culling the clustering logic is culling/ignoring vertices in a way that I cannot figure out and I do not understand the clustering algorithm or logic involved. Here is a clip with the above "fix" in Forward+ and unlike in Mobile you can see that it's not the light's distance from the camera that's causing this but the vertices themselves (wiggling the camera just right can cause one of the wall's left vertices to light up while the other is still unlit)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b1d43c90-cb96-4b05-b9a4-2ec12def1ac6

the offending code might be somewhere around line 556 in [servers/rendering/renderer_rd/forward_clustered/scene_forward_clustered.glsl](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/forward_clustered/scene_forward_clustered.glsl#L556) but this is way above my head and my best guess is that it's "ignoring" lighting for those vertices it deems not important or lit even when they should be updated with lighting.

I have added my first pull request that applies the mentioned band-aid fix of exposing an extra cull margin for lights, though this only fixes the issue in the Compatibility and Mobile renderers. The reason this does not fix the issue in the Forward+ renderer is due to it running its own culling logic during cluster building. Digging through the source has helped me confirm my theories and this isn't a "bug" in the traditional sense but rather a misunderstanding of how vertex lighting works. It might be more useful to make a new issue now that I know what exactly is causing this and what it would take to fix it. (Thoughts?) The TLDR is that due to vertex lighting being interpolated across the mesh's polygons it could have lighting far outside the light's actual radius. This problem gets worse and worse the larger the polygon is in relation to the camera, with a small or dense mesh showing little to no issue with this while a large mesh with few polygons gets the worst of it. In short, low poly meshes suffer from this the most. Right now the only metric Godot uses to cull lights are their radius (omni lights) and cone (spot lights) which is not enough information to avoid this issue. This is extra bad in the clustered renderer because the light is assigned to a cluster based on its radius when it could potentially affect many clusters outside of the radius. My proposal for fixing this in the Forward+ renderer is to introduce a new codepath in [scene_forward_clustered.glsl](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/forward_clustered/scene_forward_clustered.glsl) to bypass clustering if vertex lighting is on and render it the same way Mobile does, thus receiving the same benefit from the extra cull margin. The extra cull margin lets the user set the margin to the size of their largest polygon edge which does take manual effort but solves the problem entirely.

My PR does only fix Mobile and Compatibility and I've spoken to @clayjohn about what it would take to make it work for the Forward+ renderer and it does not seem likely to ever happen due to how the clustering works (in other words, vertex lighting will always be largely incompatible with Forward+)

As for whether it's a fix or a "fix" you're right that the user themselves have to tweak the cull margin per light but if you think about what's causing the issue (distance between vertices in a mesh affected by the light) this is not a problem that can be solved in any other way short of just disabling culling of lights in general (which my PR lets you do by just making the cull distance infinitely large) or by constantly analyzing the distance between vertices in all meshes in the scene affected by each light (unrealistic, very silly).

It's very frustrating to me that right now vertex lighting is effectively broken on all renderers and while my fix doesn't solve every problem imaginable it does make vertex lights usable on 2 out of 3 renderers.
